conflicts.point: Foundation model developers deploy trade secrecy and end-user license agreements as structural liability shields, shifting tangible operational risks onto downstream operators and injured plaintiffs.

positions.stance: Developers intentionally use licensing restrictions and trade secrecy to insulate themselves from tort exposure while shifting all legal and financial risk onto downstream deployers and injured plaintiffs.
Trade secrecy protects proprietary intellectual property and enables competitive software markets rather than serving as a malicious liability shield.

conflicts.point: Upstream liability mandates impose asymmetric fixed costs that choke open-source diffusion, whereas anchoring strict liability at the downstream market-entry act prevents offshore evasion without killing permissionless innovation.

positions.stance: Upstream mandates impose fixed costs that consolidate code ownership among large corporate incumbents and drive open-source developers offshore.
Downstream-only liability leaves enterprise buyers holding entire liability burdens without internal model visibility, creating an enforcement vacuum.

verdicts.conflict: Foundation model developers deploy trade secrecy and end-user license agreements as structural liability shields, shifting tangible operational risks onto downstream operators and injured plaintiffs.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic position provides concrete evidence by citing specific practices at firms like OpenAI and Anthropic, whereas the accelerationist claim remains an abstract defense of intellectual property. Developers routinely use end-user license agreements to disclaim operational liabilities while withholding the internal weights necessary for third-party auditing.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that standard commercial licensing agreements routinely transfer enforceable indemnification and adequate audit rights to downstream buyers.

verdicts.conflict: Upstream liability mandates impose asymmetric fixed costs that choke open-source diffusion, whereas anchoring strict liability at the downstream market-entry act prevents offshore evasion without killing permissionless innovation.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic position accounts for the enforcement vacuum created when liability is placed entirely on downstream actors who possess zero internal visibility into model architectures. While upstream mandates do impose compliance costs, downstream-only rules leave injured plaintiffs with no solvent defendant if the downstream deployer is an undercapitalized shell company.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Proof that mandatory downstream escrow mechanisms can provide adequate technical oversight without requiring upstream developers to disclose proprietary weights.
